claims.statement: A BFF Redis session record is a five-field, tokenless value (`sessionId`, `userId`, `createdAt`, `lastActivityAt`, `expiresAt`) whose idle window, absolute lifetime and per-user concurrency are tracked entirely independently of the Keycloak JWT's own expiry: `createSession(userId, tokens)` sets `lastActivityAt = createdAt = now` and `expiresAt = now + env.sessionAbsoluteTimeoutMs` and then seals the member's tokens into a separate Redis value beside the record, so the record itself never holds token material and no code path creates a session without tokens.

`cache-service.ts` keeps a session under three Redis keys — `session:<sessionId>` (the JSON record), `session-tokens:<sessionId>` (the sealed tokens), and `user-sessions:<userId>` (a set of that user's session IDs maintained with `SADD`/`SREM`) — and every TTL is derived from the session's remaining absolute lifetime by `sessionTtlSeconds()` (floored at 1s), never a fixed value, so the Redis TTL can never be shorter than the configured idle/absolute policy. A corrupt or truncated stored record is treated as no session: `parseSession()` deletes the bad key and returns null rather than throwing.

`readLiveSession(sessionId)` is the session read authority and returns a discriminated union — `{ session }`, `{ expired: 'absolute' | 'idle'; userId }`, or `{ expired: 'missing' }` — decided by a shared private `expiryOf()` that checks the absolute timeout before the idle timeout, so a session past its maximum lifetime is reported as `absolute` even when it is also idle; it deletes the session on either expiry but not when the record is missing. `readLiveSessionWithTokens()` applies the same decision after one `MGET` over the record and the tokens key (and returns `tokensRaw: null` for a pre-085 session). `getValidSession()` survives only as a thin wrapper that collapses every non-live outcome to `null` and now has no production caller, which is why the comment in `cache-service.ts` still naming it 'the authority' for idle/absolute expiry is stale.

`createSession()` enforces the per-user concurrent-session cap in two steps: a pre-add count check that evicts when the count is already at or above `MAX_SESSIONS`, then, after the record and its sealed tokens are cached, a trim loop that re-reads the count and keeps evicting while it exceeds the cap. The loop's no-progress guard (`if (next >= count) break`) exists because the `user-sessions:<userId>` set can retain members whose `session:` object is already gone, and `evictOldestSession()` returns early when no valid session is found — without the break the loop could spin without the count ever falling. The post-add trim is what makes the cap hold under simultaneous logins, since the pre-add check alone is TOCTOU-racy (feature 009 FR-018).

Eviction removes the valid session with the smallest `lastActivityAt` (sort ascending, take the first) — the least-recently-active session, which is not necessarily the oldest by `createdAt` — and `MAX_SESSIONS` is bound once at module load from `env.maxConcurrentSessions` (`MAX_CONCURRENT_SESSIONS`, default 10), so changing the environment variable after the module is imported has no effect, unlike the two timeouts which `expiryOf()` reads from `env` on each check.

Every eviction emits `logger.audit('session_evicted', { userId, activeSessions, maxSessions })`, where `activeSessions` counts only the sessions that still resolved rather than the raw set cardinality, and the evicted session ID is deliberately not logged in any form — under the key name `sessionId` the logger would redact it to a constant while still tripping the `mcm-no-token-logging` SAST rule (which matches the key name), and any other key name would leak it (feature 052 FR-001/FR-004). The event exists because the cap used to fire in silence, which made 'it never fires' and 'it fires constantly' indistinguishable from outside the process.

Nothing in `session-manager.ts` verifies that a session ID belongs to the caller — it is a keyed lookup module — so ownership is enforced at the boundary in two ways. By construction, because the `mcm_session_id` cookie is the only credential: `/bff-api/auth/refresh` takes the session from the cookie and the refresh token from that session's own sealed record (a `mcm_refresh_token` cookie sent alongside is not read, and `session-tokens.renew()` still re-checks the renewed token's `sub`, revoking it and deleting the session on a mismatch), and `/bff-api/auth/logout` resolves the owner from the session its own cookie names and touches nothing when there is no cookie. Explicitly, on every authenticated request: `requireAuth()` compares the validated access token's `sub` against `session.userId` and on a mismatch terminates the session, audits `session_refresh_owner_mismatch`, clears the auth cookies and answers 401 `SESSION_OWNER_MISMATCH`.

The client holds only the opaque session ID, never a token: on web nothing is persisted client-side (the BFF's `HttpOnly` cookies are the source of truth), and on native only the opaque ID is stored in SecureStore under `mcm_session_id` as a startup hydration hint for `hasStoredSession()`, which `AuthProvider` always follows with a `/bff-api/auth/user` call before treating the user as authenticated. The ID reaches the client as both the `mcm_session_id` `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie built by `buildAuthCookies()` and the `X-Session-Id` response header on login, but only the cookie is ever read back — `extractSessionId()` reads the cookie alone, and no `Authorization: Bearer` credential is honoured in any environment (FR-008/FR-009).

Session-lifecycle behaviour is verified at three tiers. The mocked unit tier (`unit-tests/session-manager.test.ts`, `unit-tests/auth.test.ts`) pins the read outcomes, the cap arithmetic and the authenticator's ordering but can only show the code agrees with its own model. `tests/integration/session-manager.integration.test.ts` and `tests/integration/concurrent-session-cap.integration.test.ts` run against real Redis (db 1) to prove the cap holds under a race, that the stored TTL exceeds the configured idle window, and that the eviction audit carries no session ID. `tests/integration/session-token-custody.integration.test.ts` is HTTP-level against the running BFF, real Keycloak and the BFF's Redis, covering sign-in, server-side renewal, sign-out and the refusal of a foreign sealed record. The retired `unit-tests/session-timeout.test.ts` is gone with the module it tested.

The timeout is enforced inside `requireAuth()` in `bff-server/auth.ts`, which every authenticated route calls, and the ordering is the contract: read the session and its sealed tokens in one `MGET`, refuse a missing session as 401 `SESSION_NOT_FOUND` with no audit, audit `session_expired` with `reason: 'absolute'` or `'idle'` and answer 401 `SESSION_ABSOLUTE_TIMEOUT` / `SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT` (clearing the auth cookies in each case), terminate a session whose sealed record is absent or will not open and answer 401 `SESSION_NOT_FOUND`, renew the tokens if due, validate the access token and compare its `sub` to the session owner, and only then slide the idle window with `touchSession()`. The old `bff-server/session-timeout.ts` and its `validateSessionTimeout()` are gone.

Because `requireAuth()` ends with `touchSession()` after validating the token and the owner, the idle window slides on every authenticated request, not only on the routes that read the session explicitly; `/bff-api/auth/refresh` is the second caller, sliding the window after `ensureFreshTokens(..., { force: true })`. `touchSession()` writes through `touchSessionRecord()`, which uses `SET ... EX <ttl> XX` — the session record only, and only if it still exists — so a touch racing a renewal cannot write a pre-renewal refresh token back over a rotated one (the tokens live in their own key) and a touch racing a logout cannot re-create the record the logout deleted. The `user-sessions:<userId>` set's TTL is refreshed only by `cacheSession()` on a new login, not by a touch.

The member's access and refresh tokens live beside the session as a third Redis value (`session-tokens:<sessionId>`) holding `{v, accessExpiresAt, refreshExpiresAt, blob}`, where the blob is AES-256-GCM-sealed under `AGENT_CONFIG_ENC_KEY` with an AAD bound to the session id and owner; the two expiry times sit in clear outside the ciphertext so a test can age a session without the key, while the JWT's own `exp` is still validated on every request. Renewal happens at most once per session at a time: a request that finds the access token within 30s of expiry takes the `session-renew:<sessionId>` NX lock and renews, and a concurrent request waits for the winner's tokens rather than renewing a second time (Keycloak rotates refresh tokens, so a second renewal would end the session). A session with no tokens value, or one whose record will not open for that session and owner, is never migrated — it is terminated and refused (FR-022).

The concurrent-session cap is enforced only by eviction, never by refusal: `login+api.ts` calls `getActiveSessionCount()` purely to log a non-fatal warning and records that eviction happens inside `createSession`, and although `AuthErrorCode.SESSION_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` exists it is never thrown by any code path, so a member whose oldest session is evicted is told nothing.

The client-side idle/absolute timer in `hooks/use-session-timeout.ts` (defaults 30 min / 24 h, commented as needing to match the BFF) is a prompt rather than the enforcement: it is mounted in the authenticated layout behind `isAuthenticated`, wired to `AuthProvider.logoutWithTimeout`, which records the reason for the login screen's message and then POSTs `/bff-api/auth/logout`. Its absolute timer starts at hook mount rather than at session creation, so a reload restarts the 24-hour countdown and the server's `expiresAt` remains authoritative; the `EXPO_PUBLIC_DEV_*_TIMEOUT_OVERRIDE_MS` variables shorten the client timers for E2E flows without changing what the BFF enforces.
